This is one of the best CRPG's I have ever played. The story driven content, the ability to scale difficulty around your playstyle, you can go with easy combat to make the game more story driven, or you can go tactician or honor mode for hard core, mechanically optimized combat for those who like a challenge. Larian added a lot of nice environmental interaction in the combat to the DnD rules / engine to give it more world immersion and depth in combat. The NPCs have meaningful stories and dialogue and different outcomes for different playthroughs. While I have almost 3k hours logged, half of that time is idle due to the low stress, low intensity of non-honor mode runs I can go afk for hours due to household priorities / interruptions. It is the perfect game for RPG and DnD fans.

This is my first D&D game ever, and I'll be honest: the first ten hours were rough. Turn-based combat, dice rolls, spell slots, advantage and disadvantage, none of it made sense to me at the start. I almost bounced off it.

I'm glad I pushed through. Once the systems click, the core gameplay becomes genuinely addictive. Every fight is a puzzle with ten different solutions. You can talk your way out, sneak past, shove someone off a cliff, or set the ground on fire and watch the chaos. The game reacts to almost everything you try, which is exactly what makes it so hard to put down.

And the amount of content is insane. Three massive acts, companions with real stories, choices that actually matter, and so many ways to build your character and approach every situation that I was planning a second playthrough before finishing my first.

If you've never touched D&D or a CRPG before, don't let that scare you off. The learning curve is real, but it's absolutely worth it. One of the best games I've ever played.

As someone who really likes DND, Baldur's Gate 3 is basically as close to the tabletop as you can get and play digitally. The characters, be it important or minor NPCs are full of personality and the world building is very detailed. While yes, the rules are a bit different to cater to casual fans of the game or people who only got the game due to popularity, it brings a perfect balance of the two.

This game values player's freedom of choice a lot, therefore every playthrough is unique. Consistently runs well with minor to no bugs or issues despite big game size even on lower end devices in rendering the game. Wide range of settings to accommodate all hardware. Built in modding marketplace is already a huge bonus, offering the game even more replayability and fun. The co-op mode is pretty solid.

The combat may not be everyone's thing, as it is turn-based. But it does offer a wide variety of moves and combinations which even are affected by the position of the map and your surroundings, making immersion even better. Difficulty can be changed mid-combat if it ever becomes too hard, which is a nice touch. The combat is a 9/10. Sometimes minor bugs may happen.


The story is great. Gives special interactions and shifts the narrative based on your choices to change the experience. Act 1 is definitely the most memorable, and while Act 2 does get a bit monotone the immense flood of new content in Act 3 makes up for it. I rate the main story an 8/10.

 The game features over 10 days wroth of nonstop voiced dialogue, highly detailed and well-written characters, fun combat mechanics. Good world building. Even if you don't care about that, getting it for the character customization is worth it alone for authors/artists. For characters, most of the ones available to be added to your party are romanceable, which is a good way of learning their individual backstories. These are well-thought out and incorporated into the main story. They also provide more information about the lore.



For the price of the game, it is worth your money. Especially if it goes on sale; it didn't win game of the year for nothing. Very replayable, entertaining. Graphics are good, mechanics are fun, settings accommodating. Characters are well-thought out, full of life, and their own and the main story is well-written. The world is detailed and fun to explore. Highly recommended, 9.5/10 if not 10/10 game.

Finally, I've completed this massive and immersive RPG combined with incredibly fun gameplay with around 150hrs playtime (it's 200ish hrs on Steam cause I did a lot of save scumming and AFK). Now, I get it why this game won GOTY back in 2023. This is the most beginner-friendly CRPG I've played so far, at least compared to DOS2 and Pathfinder WOTR. At first, it really looks very complex and deep, but after playing it for a while turns out its really not that difficult. The character creation is fine, there are a lot of classes and races that we can choose but not that much that it becomes overwhelming like Pathfinder WOTR. You can also multiclass in this game that makes experimenting with builds so much fun, and I'm also thinking you can build a character on your own without looking up builds on the internet without worrying your character doesn't do enough damage.

The thing I liked the most from this game would be the story and the freedom of choices you have. You can be good, evil, or neutral, everything, and every choice you made feels like it has consequences. The companion stories are also memorable, especially Shadowheart and Astarion, also their voice acting is incredible. No wonder Astarion's voice actor won the Best Performance at TGA 2023. For the combat, i think it's not bad although the combat in DOS2 felt more interactive. Anyway, overall I'm very satisfied and the game exceeded my expectations after I've played DOS2. Definitely would play another playthrough, even I've already planned what I'm gonna do in the next playthrough. I'm getting more and more excited for the next Larian Studios' CRPG, Divinity.

I’ve finished Baldur’s Gate 3 and I had a great time. This game is absolutely amazing. A true masterpiece — a gem that’s hard to come across these days. It feels like a game made by gamers, for gamers.

I had never played any of the previous Baldur’s Gate games and I wasn’t familiar with D&D mechanics. I had heard that BG3 was a great game, but I didn’t want to play another game like Divine Divinity, so I kept putting it off for over three years. My friends strongly recommended it, so I finally decided to give it a try.

And what can I say? This game is a masterpiece.

Pros:
- Great graphics
- Great music
- Excellent gameplay
- Engaging story
- No excessive political correctness — the game doesn’t shy away from brutality
- Quite expensive for a three-year-old game, but absolutely worth the money

Cons:
- It does feel a bit like Divinity at times
- Occasional bugs and crashes
- Larian’s approach of putting garbage trash everywhere. Larian’s approach of putting chests, loot, and random junk everywhere means I end up running around like a scrap collector: loot, sell, loot, sell, loot, sell, over and over again.
- By the end of the game, I had several hundred items that I never used 
- I had more money than I could possibly spend

I tend to play games by exploring absolutely everything and collecting everything I can find. While this is fun to some extent, it also takes a lot of time and, in the end, doesn’t really add that much to the experience. It’s great that there are so many hidden items, chests, and secrets, but there is honestly a bit too much of it.

I really, really enjoyed Baldur’s Gate 3. I played Divine Divinity years ago, but I didn’t really understand what was going on in the story back then.

If I had one wish, I’d say it’s a shame that Larian is working on another Divinity game instead of a new Baldur’s Gate. Larian put an enormous amount of work and effort into BG3, and it really shows.

For me, this is a masterpiece — the kind of game that is very hard to find these days. It has some minor bugs and occasional crashes, but those are nothing compared to everything the game does right.

Baldur’s Gate 3: 10/10 — I Came Here to Save the World, Not Start a Dating Scandal

I bought Baldur’s Gate 3 expecting an epic fantasy RPG where I’d battle monsters, make difficult moral choices, and occasionally save the world.

Instead, I apparently walked into Faerûn looking like the last handsome person alive.

Everyone is trying to get with me.

The vampire wants me.
The wizard wants me.
The tiefling wants me.
The goth cleric definitely wants me.
The druid wants me.
Random people I’ve known for approximately 14 seconds want me.

At this point, I’m afraid to make eye contact with an NPC because apparently that counts as foreplay.

I’ll be standing there covered in goblin blood, wearing mismatched armor, carrying 37 rotten potatoes, and someone will stroll up like, “I’ve been thinking about you…”

MY BROTHER IN MYSTRA, WE JUST MET.

Meanwhile, I’m trying to save the world while managing the most aggressively horny adventuring party in recorded history. Every long rest feels less like setting up camp and more like opening a fantasy Tinder app.

And somehow, despite all the flirting, chaos, trauma, questionable decisions, and people trying to climb into my bed, the characters are genuinely lovable. The writing is fantastic, the world is absurdly immersive, and every decision feels like it could either change the fate of Faerûn or accidentally start another romance.

10/10.

Would save the world again.

Would absolutely not make eye contact with anyone at camp afterward.

Buy it, play it, have a good time.

Also, Larian did recently put out that new Divinity trailer, and with it the proposition of GenAI assets/concept art. If this comes to fruition I will 100% lose all the love for Larian that BG3 inspired in me. PLEASE do not disappoint your fanbase.

160 hours spent playing this game! That says a lot. I was already playing it back when it wasn’t fully polished yet—bugs, crashes, optimization issues—but that didn’t stop me (reminds me of the Gothic 1 Remake). The world is simply massive: the quests are varied, there are tons of possibilities, and your actions lead to a sea of different paths and outcomes. 
As for drawbacks, I’d point out just one—the “medium” difficulty (it’s definitely not “medium/balanced”), and it might be a problem for you because battles can drag on, and getting defeated after 20 minutes of fighting really stings (and I wouldn’t exactly call myself a fan of Souls-like games).
But despite these minor flaws, just the thought of how much effort and hard work went into this game is simply mind-blowing and truly captures the imagination.

I definitely recommend it. Take some time off and enjoy a great story.

P.S. My respect to Neil Newbon, who voiced Astarion.

81 hours in. Haven’t even made it to the city of Baldur’s Gate yet. Will I be there soon? No. Have I had an incredible time? Absolutely.

I seem to be in the rare minority of people who just can't get into this game. 

Nearly 40 hours put into the game and I can't get through the first Act, not because of difficulty, but because I just don't like the characters or the story enough to care about any of it. The writing for character interactions feels like a mix of horny teen Tumblr blog and the Witcher TV show after Cavill left. 

Everything about this game just feels like the same "Trying to be Hollywood" spectacle chasing that the AAA game industry has been doing for years, and it is a full miss for me. There are no aspects of the game that I found enjoyable enough to push past the first Act, and I wish I could refund it since I will never finish it.

Plenty of other people have a very different opinion and experience with the game than I do though, so take my complete disdain and distaste for BG3 with a grain of salt. 

All in all, if you like D&D 5e, you may like this game, though I'd recommend Solasta: Crown of the Magister for a better D&D-esque experience.

I’ve put countless hours into RPGs over the years, but what Larian Studios has achieved here isn’t just impressive—it’s historical. A milestone for other devs and companies to aim for. It has to be the new standard after all these years of greedy corporate games. Baldur’s Gate 3 for me is, plain and simple, one of the greatest role-playing games ever created.

So let me give you an overview across different categories, for those who still haven't bought it (INSERT JUST DO IT MEME HERE) or who just want to read the experience of a guy who is deeply in love with this game. Just a small reminder: English is not my main language, so please excuse any minor spelling or grammar mistakes. At least it’s AI-free and written straight from the heart. I literally took 30 minutes to write and think about how to word it.

[list]
[*] [b]Story & Narrative (100% Spoiler-Free):[/b]
The narrative pulls you in from the very first minute. Every reaction, decision, and action can and will impact the story, the characters, and sometimes even the world itself. A lot of RPGs only give you the illusion of choice, but in BG3, your decisions actually carry real weight.

Sure, you can't change EVERYTHING in the game, but you have an insane amount of freedom. Are you going to be good, evil, or somewhere within the 100 shades of grey in between? Which path will you follow? Depending on how you act, your relationships with companions evolve organically, shift radically, or fall apart entirely. It never feels like you're just following a rigid script; you're actively shaping your own unique journey. The replayability is off the charts.

Also, this might be the first RPG where I didn't skip even the minor dialogue because it’s so immensely well-written. The cutscenes are top-notch, and the tabletop Pen-and-Paper feel makes it even more immersive. My personal advice: DO NOT QUICKSAVE/QUICKLOAD every "bad" die roll! You will be so much more immersed if you just live with the consequences. (Sure, on your first run you might want specific outcomes, but trust me on this tip.) Furthermore, EVERY character is exceptionally designed and written—down to the smallest NPC.

[*] [b]Unrivaled Creativity & Character Building:[/b]
If you love theorycrafting and tweaking mechanics, this game is absolute heaven. The character creation and build variety are insanely deep, but what really sets BG3 apart is how much freedom it gives you to solve problems.

There are virtually no artificial walls holding back your ingenuity. If you sit there thinking, [i]"Wait, can I actually use this spell, combine it with the environment, and bypass this entire scenario?"[/i]—almost every single time, the game lets you do it. Whether you're fine-tuning synergies between classes, talking your way out of situations that look like guaranteed fights, or coming up with completely unhinged tactical maneuvers, the game constantly respects your intelligence. It never forces you into one "correct" way to play; it gives you a massive toolbox and lets you go wild. (And trust me, I spent 20% of my playtime in character creation planning and testing builds. Call me an addict.)

[*] [b]Soundtrack & Atmosphere:[/b]
The audio design and world-building are on a completely different level. Borislav Slavov put together a soundtrack that literally stays in your head for weeks.

What makes it so good is how seamlessly the music shifts with the mood. One minute you’re sitting at a quiet campfire talking to your companions with a soft, melancholic melody in the background, and the next you’re thrown into a massive boss battle with full orchestral power and vocals that give you absolute chills. Every region feels distinct, every fight has impact, and the sound design carries the emotional weight of the game perfectly. MAN... that first big fight in the tutorial with that track blasting? HOLY GOOSEBUMPS. Everything is PEAK quality: Music, Voice Acting, Ambience—everything.

[*] [b]Graphics & Visual Presentation:[/b]
Visually, this game is a massive step up for the genre. Top-down RPGs often struggle to feel cinematic, but BG3 completely changes the game with its close-up cutscenes and facial animations. Sure, it’s not mind-blowing UE5 ultra-next-gen graphics, but it looks fantastic, and there are great texture mods available if you want even more crispness.

The attention to detail in the world design is insane—from the dynamic lighting hitting dense forests to the intricate armor textures and spell effects popping off in combat. Even subtle character expressions during dialogue carry emotional weight, making every conversation feel like a high-budget cinematic experience rather than just reading lines of text.

[*] [b]Moddability & Personalization:[/b]
Even in its vanilla state, BG3 is a masterpiece, but the modding potential takes this game straight into infinite replayability territory. Larian backing official mod integration—alongside the insane work the community does on third-party tools—makes customizing your experience seamless.

I’ve personally sunk countless hours into building, testing, and fine-tuning my own custom mod list just to get the mechanics, visual fidelity, and difficulty balancing exactly where I want them. It’s gotten to the point where the guys in my Discord literally started calling me the "Mod Father."

That said, a quick word of advice: curate with care. The modding scene is massive, which means for every incredible quality-of-life tweak, immersive spell pack, or tactical overhaul, there are plenty of cringey, immersion-breaking mods out there that ruin the atmosphere. But if you take the time to build a clean, grounded setup, you can turn an already legendary RPG into your own tailored masterpiece.

[*] [b]Final Verdict & Studio Trust:[/b]
Look, I know how this sounds. Reading through all of this, you might think I’m just some blind Larian fanboy who hypes up anything they drop. I’m really not. I’ve been gaming for way too long, and I’m usually the first person to criticize studios when they get lazy or greedy.

The reality is that BG3 simply earned every single bit of praise it gets. Larian gave haters and cynical critics zero room to hit them with legitimate bashing. In an era where the industry is clogged with half-baked releases, predatory microtransactions, battle passes, and empty live-service promises, Larian (alongside CD Projekt Red) stands as one of the very few AAA studios left that I actually trust. You can feel the sheer love, sweat, and respect for the player packed into every single frame of this game.
[/list]

[b]Final Words:[/b]
If you don't have BG3 in your library yet: [u]Buy it.[/u] It doesn't matter if you think turn-based combat isn't your thing—this is an absolute MUST-PLAY milestone in gaming history.

My first RPG ever, and it set the bar incredibly high.
I finished the game on Tactician difficulty after switching from Balanced because the combat became too easy. That was the right decision—boss fights like Raphael, Ansur, Orin, and the Netherbrain became memorable tactical encounters instead of simple damage races.
The biggest strength of Baldur's Gate 3 isn't just the story. It's how every system works together: companions, choices, combat, exploration, dialogue, and progression. I never felt forced into one solution, and almost every quest rewarded creativity.
I also played it under the best possible conditions: 4K, GeForce NOW Ultimate, and AI available whenever I needed clarification about mechanics or lore without spending hours searching through wikis. It made the experience smooth while still letting me make my own decisions.
One thing I appreciate the most is that I finished a 100+ hour RPG without feeling burned out or addicted. I simply enjoyed the journey.
I probably won't replay it because the first playthrough is what makes this game truly special, and I want to keep those memories intact.
For me, this is one of the best games ever made.

I really wanted to like this game. Spent so long with my friends trying to get a campaign going. We tried with 4 people and after months and months of aligning schedules and starting multiple campaigns I decided it just is not meant to be played with more than 2 people on your first run.

So I tried it solo and for the first couple hours it was so much better. I tried tactical difficulty and after dying a few times it felt like my decisions in character specs and party config actually mattered. But after failing repeatedly in a couple fights against higher-level opponents I realized a lot of the time, winning and losing was less about skill and more about going back and gaining experience to buff your crew.

It's an RPG and some grind to beef up your characters is totally expected. The problem is that for me, the story elements were so slow and not rewarding. The little amount of strategy sprinkled in was too few and far between bland dialogue trees. So many story beat payoffs felt like just edgy sex jokes involving fantasy creatures.

The conversation around this game is so positive and I've never heard anyone talk about the downsides of multiplayer in this game so I'm very disappointed with it. We wanted an online D&D-type experience, and it just fundamentally fails counts of 3 or more new players. Even solo I got only a few hours of entertaining game play, but I believe the right people would enjoy it solo. I imagine for those who play it solo, you could then have fun playing with others who have already beaten the game. But starting fresh with multiple people ruins the experience. If players wander to different places, they start and end quests independently, and trying to enforce your party staying together is extremely difficult because listening to every conversation and waiting for the speaker to choose their dialogue is tedious. So you either have sessions where almost nothing happened and everyone sat around or you have sessions where you feel like things have happened randomly and you don't know what's going on.

Without a doubt the greatest CRPG game I have ever played. Totally engrossing. This captures D&D. For me RPGs start with D&D. It is the genesis of the rpg. It has evolved into this game. 

A lot of choices to be made. First was my character. A barbaric berzerker Green Dragonborn. Couldn't be happier with my choice.  I think it made my build more interesting for me. I view him more as an extremely violent evolved bipedal reptilian man. Loved using it's ability to spray acid. Used this ability numerous times in crowed doorways full of enemies. Watched five of them drop dead at one time because of previous damage done.  One of my tactics is getting NPCs to crowd a doorway and be in a position where the party can't be flanked. I thought I have Godzilla here. Have a lot of time invested in this character. His name is Drahgos.

The later choices after were the consuming of the tadpoles and the Illithid powers you receive. Another dimension to the game. I have all of the Illithid powers. Including the expanded ones. You can say my character went to the dark side.  I thought my character is Darth Vader now serving his own emperor. So I might as well run with it. Probably what inspired this choice for the developers.  And now a Chosen Slayer of Bhaal himself. I have thought how does my character reconcile having two masters when the rule is a man cannot have two masters? This character is his own master and does what is in his interest which is the completing of the campaign/quest. They are just a means to an end. Just as my character is to them. His loyalty is to Astarion, Gale and Lae'zel. The developers play on this.  The Illithid powers made the character more deadly. IMO the Psionic Backlash, Psionic Dominance, and fly are the best. But the most deadly is Cull the Weak. If an NPC is within 40-60 hit points there is a good chance they will be killed by my Hammer of Justice or by my Dwarven Thrower in one strike with rage. The emersion I love when it comes to an CRPG.   

All of this sets the stage for the best moment I ever had with CRPGs. Was in the Bhaal temple and not being able to make it past the Bhaal assassins and their wizard that makes a lot of trouble for you. Had to do some research. Had no understanding how the spell of Unstoppable and Sanctuary worked. Don't know everything about D&D and how these spells worked and how to do damage to the assassins while they are invisible and using the Sanctuary spell and the wizard using the Unstoppable spell.  Knowledge is power. Got creative. This one I would do solo without my party and use my Illithid powers. Go ripping off flying. Get behind the NPCs. Hit and run. With my Deathstalker cloak and getting invisibility for two turns and my Dwarven thrower after a kill with flying my character was a nightmare. Didn't have to use rage on my first dozen culls. I would just be burning them up going in and out of turned based combat. No NPC got a strike in on me until the Bhaal assassins popped up. The elixir of See Invisibility doesn't give you the ability to see everything.  Got the drop on two of them that were visible to me. Flew right to them.  Smashed them both with two strikes from my Hammer of Justice. Went invisible and flew away both times still keeping conscious of the wizard. Then it was cat and mouse. The AI knew what I was doing and set a trap for me in the building with the next two. They did some damage that put me on edge. Thought I was removed and safe from them. They nailed me good. Then went away to different parts in the building. Bottom and top. Waited them out and observed they were going invisible in the same place trying to find me. The second time they both did that at different times threw a grenade to that spot. The Sanctuary spell does not protect the NPCs from damage that does not come from melee weapons and spells. Done and dead. Then it was the wizards turn. Found a point where I could shoot my bolts from my Harold crossbow at him while he was high on his perch. Had the Unstoppable Spell down to one more hit and he was open for damage next turn. He came down looking for me. Big mistake. He got within a few meters from me. Fired one more bolt. The Unstoppable spell was done. Switched to my Dwarven Thrower. Scored a critical. All that action didn't give me much room to pull away with my tactics. He advanced on me again. Had a dialogue box pop before he cast his spell.  Psionic Backlash or Psionic Disruption. Picked Disruption. It worked his spell was blocked. Now it was my turn. Flew over to him and smashed him with one strike with rage still going on. In my imagination I see my character slowly descending  and the wizard knows his fate is sealed with some kind of evil operatic music going on with my character in his evil Dark Justiciar Helmet on with his dyed green armor. Darth Vader. Evil. The wizard's head is smashed with extreme force in an instant. Just like in a movie. 

How could you not love this as a gaming experience? This is the new entertainment. I have not played this kind of CRPG in years. The last time was DDO.  BG3 is a masterpiece of entertainment.

I have criticisms though. One is capping the levels off at twelve. One of the reasons I do side quests or just about any quest I can find is to level up my characters so they will better prepared for the bigger more difficult encounters that eventually come up. That is one of my strategies when playing CRPGs. We want to be at an advantage when they happen. Nothing wrong with that. CRPGs have always operated on the carrot and the stick. The biggest one is leveling up making your characters more viable and, yes, more powerful where they stand a better chance to come out of these encounters with less difficulty. It makes us feel good about our character build. I found it disappointing when I entered act three and leveled up to twelve in my first quest. Took a little air out. There should be room for more.

It is truly rare that a game captivates me as much as this one has. There was a lot of controversy when this game got released, due to how many studios kept saying that Larian had given people unrealistic expectations for what can be delivered in a game. Is that true? I'm not the one to say. But what I can say is that this game defeats every single other game in its scope, depth, and immersion. 

Never, and I mean never, have I put hundreds of hours into a game with the ability to go into a new play through and discover something that I haven't seen before and have a completely different experience from the previous. Even with 250 hours at the time of this review, I am already thinking about the things I should try in my next play through, anticipating how different it is going to be from my current one.

Baldur's Gate 3 is one of those games that will go down in history as a true masterpiece that rocked the gaming industry to its very core and showed other studios what it takes to create a truly great game. Now if you'll excuse me, I need to go stuff 100 smoke bombs in a backpack, go invisible, then throw it in Gortash's face and insta-kill him.
